questions.qtext: Which SQL statement is used to retrieve distinct values from a column?
questions.solution:
Answer: C, A

Selected solution (score: 0)
Answer is option $\boxed C$

A. SELECT UNIQUE column_name FROM table_name;

$UNIQUE$ keyword is used in different context , it returns $TRUE$ if the table on left side of $UNIQUE$ has no duplicates.

B. SELECT DIFFERENT column_name FROM table_name;

No keyword like $DIFFERENT$ exists in SQL , hence this query is wrong.

C. SELECT DISTINCT column_name FROM table_name;

This is correct query and will return Distinct column names

D. SELECT ONLY column_name FROM table_name;

Again no keyword like $ONLY$ exists in sql
Source solution 2 (score: 1)
Answer is C

The SQL standard defined DISTINCT as the keyword for fetching unique (or distinct) values.

Unique/Different/Only are not used for fetching distinct values.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are false?

options.text: Relational algebra and SQL are declarative languages.
The difference between sets and bags is that sets don't allow repeated values.
In a table with primary key $(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B})$, every value of A must be unique.
Given a relational schema, there is only one way to translate a given English query against that schema's data into a correct SQL query.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C, D

Selected solution (score: 1)

Answer is option $\boxed{A,C,D}$

Option A: No, Relational algebra is procedural Language . Hence this statement is FALSE.

Option B: This is True , sets only contains distinct values whereas Multiset(or Bag) can contain duplicate vallues.

Option C: This is false, consider a table with $(A,B)$ values being $(1,2)$ and $(1,3)$ , $A$ value is same in both tuple but still $AB$ is a primary key here. Value of $(A,B)$ toghether must be unique.

Option D: This is false, we can write multiple valid SQL query to produce the same result .

questions.qtext:
Consider the following ORACLE relations :

One $(x, y) = \{<2, 5>, <1, 6>, <1, 6>, <1, 6>, <4, 8>, <4, 8> \}$

Two $(x, y) = \{<2, 55>, <1, 1>, <4, 4>, <1, 6>, <4, 8>, <4, 8>, <9, 9>, <1, 6> \}$

Consider the following two $SQL$ queries $SQ1$ and $SQ2$ :

SQ1 : 

 (SELECT * FROM One)
 EXCEPT
 (SELECT * FROM Two);

SQ2 :

 (SELECT * FROM One)
 EXCEPT ALL
 (SELECT * FROM Two);

For each of the SQL queries, what is the cardinality (number of rows) of the result obtained when applied to the instances above ?
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 17)
Here the difference of keywords only which are "EXCEPT" and "EXCEPT ALL" in both the queries.

The EXCEPT keyword will work the same as SET DIFFERENCE of Set Theory.

So it will return 1 tuple only which is <2,5>.

The EXCEPT ALL keyword will have more to do it work on the frequency of that value, like <2,5> appears one time in relation X and <2,5> appears 0 times in relation Y. So 1 -0 = 1. so it will come into output 1 time.

Now <1,6> appears 3 times in relation X and 2 times in relation Y so 3 - 2 = 1, so in the output it will come 1 time.

In the output, we will get {<2,5> <1,6>}, 2 tuples.

Now point to be noticed in the query we are taking all attributes so we are performing EXCEPT and EXCEPT ALL operations on all the attributes

Option B is correct.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following three SQL queries (Assume the data in the people table):

  1. Select Name from people where $\text{Age}>21$;
  2. Select Name from people where $\text{Height}>180$;
  3. Select Name from people where $(\text{Age}>21)$ or $(\text{Height}>180)$;

If the SQL queries $a$ and $b$ above, return $10$ rows and $7$ rows in the result set respectively, then what is one possible number of rows returned by the SQL query $c$?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 22)

Let's analyze the three SQL queries one by one:

1. Query a:

SELECT Name 
FROM People 
WHERE Age > 21;

This query returns 10 rows.

2. Query b:

 SELECT Name
 FROM People
 WHERE Height > 180;

This query returns 7 rows.

3. Query c: 

SELECT Name 
FROM People 
WHERE Age > 21 OR Height > 180;

This query will return rows where either the age is greater than 21 or the height is greater than 180, or both.

To determine the possible number of rows returned by query c, we need to consider the overlap between the two conditions:

Let \( A \) be the set of rows where Age > 21 (10 rows).
Let \( B \) be the set of rows where Height > 180 (7 rows).
Let \( A \cup B \) be the set of rows where either condition is true.

The number of rows returned by query c is the size of \( A \cup B \). Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion, we can express the size of \( A \cup B \) as:

\[ |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| \]

Where \( |A \cap B| \) is the number of rows that satisfy both conditions.

Given:
\( |A| = 10 \)
\( |B| = 7 \)

The minimum possible value for \( |A \cup B| \) occurs when there is maximum overlap between the two sets, i.e., \( |A \cap B| \) is at its maximum. In this case, \( |A \cap B| = 7 \).

So, the minimum possible value of \( |A \cup B| \):

\[ |A \cup B| = 10 + 7 - 7 = 10 \]

The maximum possible value for \( |A \cup B| \) occurs when there is no overlap between the two sets, i.e., \( |A \cap B| = 0 \).

So, the maximum possible value of \( |A \cup B| \):

\[ |A \cup B| = 10 + 7 - 0 = 17 \]

So, any value between 10 and 17 (inclusive) is possible, depending on the actual overlap in the data.

Therefore Option C is correct

Source solution 2 (score: 0)
Since in each of i, ii, iii SELECT clauses, DISTINCT is NOT used, so we can consider each of them as a set.

i.e., |i| = 10 and |ii| = 7

Now | i U ii | = range of [10, 17]

questions.qtext:
Consider a database table T containing two columns $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$ each of type $\text{integer}$. After the creation of the table, one record $\text{(X=1, Y=1)}$ is inserted in the table.

Let $\text{MX}$ and $\text{MY}$ denote the respective maximum values of $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$ among all records in the table at any point in time. Using $\text{MX}$ and $\text{MY}$, new records are inserted in the table $128$ times with $\text{X}$ and $\text{Y}$ values being $\text{MX+1, 2*MY+1}$ respectively. It may be noted that each time after the insertion, values of $\text{MX}$ and $\text{MY}$ change.

What will be the output of the following SQL query after the steps mentioned above are carried out?

SELECT Y FROM T WHERE X=7;
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 6)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete Analysis & Variations: https://youtu.be/zb6vXpZVo1E?t=4186&feature=shared

Assume $n$ new tuples are inserted, & If query asks $sum(X), sum(Y)$, then:

$Sum(X) = (n+1)(n+2)/2$

$Sum(Y) = 2(2^{n+1}-1) - (n+1)$

Source of the question: https://gateoverflow.in/2134/gate-cse-2011-question-32

If you observe the pattern here carefully, the relation between X & Y is $Y = 2^X -1$

So, Y value when X = 7 is $2^7-1 = 127$
Answer is 127

The SQL expression

SELECT DISTINCT T.branch_name
FROM branch T, branch S
WHERE T.assets > S.assets
 AND S.branch_city = 'Mumbai';

finds the names of

options.text: All branches that have greater assets than some branch located in Mumbai
All branches that have greater assets than all branches in Mumbai
The branch that has greatest asset in Mumbai
Any branch that has greater assets than any branch in Mumbai

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 0)
Answer is option $\boxed{A}$

The query is takes 2 instances of the table branch $T$ and $S$ , do the cross product and select all those tuples in which $T.assets >S.assets$ and $S.branch='Mumbai'$. This will give us all those $T.branch\_name$ which have more assets than atleast $1$ branch from mumbai.

questions.qtext:
Consider the set of relations shown below and the SQL query that follows.

Students: (Roll_number, Name, Date_of_birth)

Courses: (Course_number, Course_name, Instructor)

Grades: (Roll_number, Course_number, Grade)

Select distinct Name
from Students, Courses, Grades
where Students.Roll_number=Grades.Roll_number
 and Courses.Instructor = 'Korth'
 and Courses.Course_number = Grades.Course_number
 and Grades.Grade = 'A'

Which of the following sets is computed by the above query?

options.text: Names of students who have got an A grade in all courses taught by Korth
Names of students who have got an A grade in all courses
Names of students who have got an A grade in at least one of the courses taught by Korth

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 2)

Answer is option $\boxed{C}$

We are doing Natural join for $Courses$ and $Grades$ based on $Course\_number$ and then natural joining with $Students$ based on $Roll\_number$. Then selecting all those Distinct Name of students who scored Grade A in a course taught by Instructor 'Korth'.

Option A is false because the given sql query needs names of the student who have scored A in atleast 1 course taught by korth.
